issues.legal_issue: A writ petition challenging a tax show-cause notice should not ordinarily be entertained before the recipient responds to the notice and exhausts the available statutory remedies.
material_facts: The assessing authority issued reassessment show-cause notices after documents seized during searches at other entities’ premises were found to refer to the assessee.
The assessee obtained copies of the seized documents but filed a writ petition challenging the notices without first submitting a reply or objections to the assessing authority.
The applicable tax law provided remedies through the assessment process and subsequent statutory forums.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have entertained the writ petition at the show-cause stage. The Supreme Court set aside its judgment, allowed the assessee time to submit objections for the assessing authority to consider before proceeding, and directed the assessee to exhaust the statutory remedies if an adverse assessment followed.
issues.legal_principle: When an effective alternative statutory remedy is available, an aggrieved party should ordinarily pursue it before invoking writ jurisdiction. At the show-cause stage, the recipient should submit a reply and raise available defences before the authority. The Court relied on Bellary Steels & Alloys Ltd. v. CCT, (2009) 17 SCC 547, and Indo Asahi Glass Co. Ltd. v. ITO, (2002) 10 SCC 444. It did not decide the correctness of the High Court’s interpretation of Section 153C of the Income Tax Act, 1961.

predicates.writ_challenges_tax_show_cause_notice: The proceeding is a writ petition challenging a tax authority’s show-cause notice.
predicates.alternative_statutory_remedy_available: The person receiving the notice can raise objections with the authority and pursue remedies through the statutory process.
predicates.no_reply_before_writ: The person receiving the notice seeks writ relief without first submitting a reply or objections to the authority.

issues.definition: When a writ petition challenges a tax show-cause notice, a statutory remedy is available, and the recipient has not replied to the notice, the writ should not be entertained before that remedy is exhausted.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court need not reopen tax assessment outcomes that the lower appellate bodies resolved primarily on the facts when no substantial question of law requires decision.
material_facts: In the related appeals, the First Appellate Authority, the Tribunal, and the High Court had concluded on the facts of each case that the assessing authority was not justified in computing the assessments and imposing tax and interest liability.
The Supreme Court found no substantial question of law requiring decision in those appeals.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not interfere with those fact-based outcomes and disposed of the appeals without an order as to costs.
issues.legal_principle: Where the First Appellate Authority, the Tribunal, and the High Court have decided the matter primarily on its facts, and no substantial question of law requires decision, the Supreme Court need not decide a further legal question or disturb those outcomes. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.

predicates.tax_appeal_from_assessment_liability: The proceeding is an appeal concerning tax assessments and resulting liability.
predicates.lower_bodies_decided_primarily_on_facts: The appellate authorities below reached their conclusions primarily by assessing the facts of the cases.
predicates.no_substantial_question_of_law_identifie: The Supreme Court finds no substantial question of law requiring decision.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning tax assessment liability, when the lower bodies decided primarily on the facts and no substantial question of law is identified, the Supreme Court declines to reopen the fact-based outcome.
